summary: Updates the EAP applicability statement from RFC 3748 to reflect how EAP is now used in the Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond web (ABFAB) architecture. It does not change how EAP itself works.

eli5.summary: The rulebook for a login method needs a note saying it is also used in a new place.

questions: what is the eap applicability statement
why does eap need channel binding
can eap be used for application authentication
subtitle: EAP is no longer only for network access: when it guards applications, channel bindings become mandatory.

tldr.problem: The EAP applicability statement in RFC 3748 limited EAP to network access authentication, but EAP is now also used to authenticate access to applications, including in federated settings spanning several organizations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7057 appends new text to the statement. When EAP is used for application authentication, EAP channel bindings are REQUIRED on the peer and server, the application must define its own binding attributes, and the protocol carrying EAP must prove possession of the EAP Master Session Key (MSK).
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3748 without changing how EAP itself works. Applications are also told to decide for themselves how to handle retransmission, discarded messages and re-authentication.

today: RFC 7057 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2013 that updates RFC 3748. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Statement Needed an Update
sections.content:
The applicability statement in RFC 3748 says that the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is "for use in network access authentication, where IP layer connectivity may not be available". It also says that using EAP for other purposes, such as bulk data transport, is NOT RECOMMENDED.

RFC 7057 keeps some of the reasons behind that advice, but finds other provisions too narrow. Its example is EAP used to authenticate access to applications, as in the Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond web (ABFAB) architecture. The RFC supplies new text to update Section 1.3, "Applicability", of RFC 3748.
sections.eli5: The old rule said this login method was only for joining networks. People started using it for apps too, so the rule needed a small addition.

sections.title: Using EAP for Application Access
sections.content:
Ongoing IETF work specifies EAP over the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) for generic application-layer access (RFC 7055). In the past, this use of EAP met resistance because there were no channel bindings (RFC 6677). Without them, a peer cannot verify whether an authenticator is authorized to provide an advertised service.

The RFC gives an example: an environment with several printers, some of which output confidential documents to a controlled location. If a peer sends a document to the wrong printer service, sensitive information might be printed in an uncontrolled place. A low-value service is also more likely to be compromised than a high-value one. If it could impersonate the high-value service, overall security would be limited by the weaker one.

The problem is most acute in a federated environment, where several organizations with different policies and goals are involved. There, authenticating the EAP server is not enough: the peer must also validate that the contacted host is authorized to provide the requested service.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending a secret note to the school office, but a stranger has put up a fake office sign. It is not enough to know the person is nice; you must know they are really the office.

sections.title: Channel Binding Requirements
sections.content:
For environments where EAP is used for purposes other than network access, the RFC sets these rules:

  • All EAP servers and all application access EAP peers MUST support channel bindings. All network access EAP peers SHOULD support them.
  • Channel binding MUST be used for all application authentication. The EAP server MUST require that the correct EAP lower-layer attribute, or another attribute indicating the purpose of the authentication, is present in the channel binding data.
  • Channel binding SHOULD be used for network access authentication. When channel binding data is present, the EAP server MUST require that it contain the correct EAP lower-layer attribute.
  • Any new usage of EAP MUST use channel bindings including the EAP lower-layer attribute, to prevent confusion with network access usage.

Operators are warned to think carefully before relaxing these rules. If channel binding is not required and EAP is introduced into an existing non-network-access service, a device can be built that impersonates a Network Access Service (NAS) to peers while proxying the authentication to the application service. That can lower the security of the service even for users who previously used non-EAP authentication.

The RFC also says it is REQUIRED for the application layer to prove that both the EAP peer and the EAP authenticator possess the EAP Master Session Key (MSK). Otherwise an attacker could insert himself into the conversation and impersonate the peer or authenticator. The application should also define channel binding attributes that show the service is correctly represented to the peer.
sections.eli5: The rule is: always check that the person you are talking to really is who they claim to be for this job, and prove you both know the same secret. Do not skip the check just because it looks fine.

sections.title: Retransmission and Discarded Messages
sections.content:
In EAP, the authenticator is responsible for retransmission. By default EAP assumes the lower layer, which here is the application, is unreliable. The authenticator can send a packet whenever its retransmission timer fires, so applications need to be able to receive and process EAP messages at any time during the conversation.

Alternatively, EAP lets a lower layer set the retransmission timer to infinite. The lower layer then becomes responsible for reliable delivery. Applications that use a lock-step or client-driven authentication protocol might benefit from this.

Some EAP methods discard erroneous input instead of answering with an error. If an attacker caused the bad input, legitimate input can sometimes arrive afterwards. Applications MUST handle discarded EAP messages, but how depends on the application. Options include failing the authentication at the application level, requesting an EAP retransmit, and waiting for more EAP input.
sections.eli5: If a letter gets lost, someone has to send it again. EAP says the checker does that by default, but an app can choose to take over the job of making sure letters arrive.

sections.title: Re-authentication
sections.content:
EAP lower layers MAY provide a way to re-authenticate within an existing session. This lets security associations be updated without setting up a new session, which matters for network access because interrupting it can disrupt connections and media.

Some applications may not need it. If sessions are short-lived or can be replaced without much disruption, a new connection may be enough. The RFC names HTTP and SMTP as protocols where establishing a new connection to refresh security associations is likely to be sufficient.

Re-authentication is likely to be valuable when sessions or connections are long-lived or costly to disrupt. It can also matter when only one party in a protocol, for example the client, is allowed to open a new connection but the other party needs the security association refreshed. Application designers must decide whether to support it and which parties can start it.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you can show your ticket again without leaving the ride. Short rides do not need that; long rides you do not want to stop might.

sections.title: The Revised Applicability Statement
sections.content:
The RFC appends new text to the applicability statement in RFC 3748. When EAP is used for application authentication, support for EAP channel bindings is REQUIRED on the EAP peer and EAP server, to validate that the host is authorized to provide the requested services. The application MUST define channel binding attributes sufficient to validate that the service is correctly represented to the peer.

The protocol carrying EAP MUST prove possession of the EAP MSK between the peer and the authenticator. For application access, the application is providing the EAP lower layer. Because application protocols vary, their transport characteristics must be considered when deciding retransmission and re-authentication behavior.

The text also notes that applications may need to convert identities from an application-specific character set to UTF-8 or another character set required by a particular EAP method.
sections.eli5: This is the actual sentence added to the old rulebook: if you use the login method for apps, you must check the app is the right one and prove you share the secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond the requirements above, applications should consider how server authentication is achieved. Some deployments may allow weak server authentication that is then validated by an additional, existing exchange providing mutual authentication.

To fully mitigate the risk of NAS impersonation in that case, it is RECOMMENDED that mutual channel bindings be used to bind the authentications together, as described in RFC 7029. When doing channel binding, it is REQUIRED that the authenticator cannot modify the channel binding data passed between the peer and the authenticator as part of authentication.
sections.eli5: If the first check of who you are talking to is weak, add a second check and tie the two together, so no one in the middle can change the details.
